title: Bank of America sends strong signal to Microsoft stock investors
detail:
Bank of America sends strong signal to Microsoft stock investors
Hillary Remy, Celine Provini
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 12:03 PM MST 5 min read
MSFT
Trade MSFT on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Microsoft has spent years building toward an enterprise AI moment it believed was coming.

The infrastructure it bet on was not a model. It was Office: a user base built up over decades, their documents, their email histories, and the workflows running through all of it.

Copilot is the product now sitting on top of that base.

Bank of America analyst Tal Liani hosted an investor session with Jacob Andreou, executive vice president of Copilot, on Nov. 20. The setup was different from a standard earnings call. Liani brought Andreou directly in front of investors to walk through where the enterprise AI strategy stands, what Microsoft is still building, and what it still needs to prove.

Liani reiterated a Buy rating on Microsoft (MSFT) with a price target of $630, against a Nov. 20 closing price of $498.30. In a note shared with TheStreet, he laid out the case Andreou made and what it means for investors watching the stock.

Why enterprise AI still depends on context more than capability

Andreou's starting point was a problem Microsoft has been pitching for a while. Frontier models score well on benchmarks. Put them inside a company with no access to its files, client histories, or the conversations employees have been having for years, and the results start to disappoint.

Also read: Microsoft CEO Nadella faces uncomfortable reality after outage

Andreou called Work IQ Copilot's intelligence layer. He described how it tracks the way work actually moves inside an organization: an email thread about a client deal, the Teams call that followed it, the files that came out of that call, all linked together. When a question touches any part of that chain, the system is built to pull it up.

The outside providers have capable models. Getting those models to understand a specific company's internal work, its email threads, project history, and files going back years, requires access Microsoft already has.

Andreou made that case at the session. The note put it at the center of Copilot's competitive position.

3 tiers and what they tell investors about how revenue scales

Andreou described three types of users, each with a different revenue profile. Starters already have basic Copilot features inside their Microsoft 365 plans. They're using the product, just not paying for it separately. Getting them to eventually buy a seat is the first conversion Microsoft is after.

Subscribers are paying for a Copilot seat. The more engaged users go further, into modules like Autopilot for background task execution, Code for building custom apps and dashboards, and Cowork for working across multiple files at once. Those modules bill on consumption, meaning Microsoft charges based on what the system actually processes.

title: AI debt fears mount: why cash and defensive stocks are back in favor

AI debt fears mount: why cash and defensive stocks are back in favor
TheStreet Staff, CutterStudios.AI, Dominic Diongson
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 11:00 AM MST 6 min read
SJM
BRK-B
AAPL
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Steep drops from all-time highs can make fallen tech leaders look cheap, particularly after a market leader has declined sharply from its high. But a lower stock price doesn't mean the industry's heavy financial bets will pay off — or that the broader market selloff is over.

Ron Insana, CEO of Insana Information Partners, is encouraging investors with heavy tech exposure to rebalance their portfolios, raise cash, and wait for clearer market signals. He suggests parking cash in three- and six-month U.S. Treasury bills for the time being, and favors companies like Berkshire Hathaway, Apple, Microsoft, and J. M. Smucker over the debt-heavy parts of the AI trade.

That strategy is intended for investors with overly concentrated portfolios or near-term cash needs. For long-term, buy-and-hold investors who have retirement money and decades before they plan to tap their funds, Insana takes a different view.

Here is how Insana, who spoke in an interview with TheStreet's Caroline Woods, separates near-term liquidity needs from long-term exposure to technology and stocks.

Why the S&P 500 can mask a deeper stock market decline

Insana's immediate concern is that major market indexes can look far healthier than the average stock. Since momentum peaked in June, he noted, roughly 40% to 50% of S&P 500 companies have fallen by 20% or more — the measure of an individual stock entering bear market territory — even while the broader index held up relatively well.

Insana argues that weakness spreads from the bottom up. If financial and tech shares falter as more stocks are already falling, the large-cap companies propping up the major indexes could be next. Still, he notes this is only a possibility. He acknowledged that his bearish call in March was wrong because the economy and market proved far more resilient than he anticipated.

For investors whose index funds have outperformed their individual stocks, Insana suggested trimming some S&P 500 exposure to reduce risk without panic-selling
the stocks that have already fallen. He frames the move not as an all-or-nothing market call, but as routine rebalancing to bring a portfolio back in line with an investor's risk tolerance.

Why AI debt matters more than a lower Nvidia share price

Insana, a former anchor on CNBC, sees the central risk in AI financing rather than in a single stock's valuation. He pointed to uncertainty over whether data-center revenue and return on invested capital, or the profit produced by money put into a business, will be sufficient to support the debt used to build AI infrastructure. He also cited growing losses at OpenAI and Anthropic despite rapidly rising revenue.

Warning for CoreWeave: Satya Nadella Says "Selling to One or Two Customers Is Not a Business" ©@Jirsak from Getty Images Pro via Canva
Key Takeaways

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said selling to one or two customers "is not a business," and that Microsoft builds its own capacity first and rents last.

That's a warning for CoreWeave, whose three biggest customers made up 72% of second-quarter revenue, and for Nebius and IREN, which count Microsoft as an anchor customer.

CoreWeave's free cash flow was negative $7.25 billion in 2025, while Microsoft spent $116 billion on capex in its latest fiscal year.

CoreWeave's customer base is broadening, but it still rests on a few big buyers, and its landlord Applied Digital carries the same risk.

Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) CEO Satya Nadella has a blunt view of companies that live off a couple of big customers.

"Just selling to one or two customers is not a business in my opinion," he said on the Nov. 18 episode of Mad Money, while explaining how Microsoft matches its spending to demand.

He didn't name anyone. But Jim Cramer's next question was about the neoclouds, and that's a problem for CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ), which leans on a few huge buyers, and for Nebius (NBIS:NASDAQ) and IREN (IREN:NASDAQ), which count Microsoft as an anchor customer. Even Applied Digital (APLD:NASDAQ), which leases its only running campus to CoreWeave, is exposed.

Cramer asked whether that's why Microsoft uses neoclouds for "a minority of your business, but still a great deal," adding: "They charge 30% more than if you build your own."

Nadella said Microsoft rented because it was short of supply. "We build, we lease, we rent. All three will always be options," he said, but "we build for the long term, we lease and then we rent."

So renting comes last. That's not great news if renting out compute is your whole business.

What Tiger's Filing Reveals and What It Leaves Out

A 13F reports quarter-end holdings, not individual trades. It does not show what price Tiger sold at, when in the quarter it sold, or why. Filings arrive about 45 days after quarter-end, so this is a September 30 snapshot and tells you nothing about Tiger's current holdings. Any story about Tiger's motivation is a guess.

The filing does show where Alphabet sits in Tiger's portfolio. The remaining stake ranked just below Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) at a 5.76% weight and far behind NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), Tiger's largest position at 13.59%. Tiger was one of several funds that cut. Among 24 tracked institutional filings, 9 reduced Alphabet while 13 added.

Alphabet's Fundamentals Tell a Split Story

Third-quarter revenue reached $127.577 billion, up 24.65% from a year earlier. Google Cloud led the gain: revenue rose 103% to $30.709 billion, and segment operating income climbed to $11.121 billion from $3.594 billion.

Musk Warns AI's "Cash Shortage Is Also Going to Be Nuts Next Year." Credit Markets Put SpaceX Beside Oracle ©NASA/Aubrey Gemignani and Nikada from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Elon Musk warned on X that AI's compute delays will take "hundreds of billions of incremental dollars just for working capital" next year.

SpaceX relies more on outside credit than its CFO's self-funding message suggests.

J.P. Morgan's credit default swap data puts SpaceX beside Oracle at about 275 basis points, against about 80 for Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon.

Analysts expect SpaceX's free cash flow to be negative $146 billion in 2027.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) CEO Elon Musk has a warning for everyone building AI data centers. It may apply to his own company most of all.

He posted on X:

"The cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year. Even cumulative industry delays of a few months between paying for compute and getting it reliable enough to generate revenue will mean hundreds of billions of incremental dollars just for working capital. Where will that come from?"

For SpaceX, credit markets have a pretty good guess: lenders.

SpaceX lands in the "credit-dependent" tier

One investor laid out J.P. Morgan's credit default swap data on X. Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), Alphabet (GOOG) and Amazon trade at about 80 basis points, "with enough cash flow to fund most of their CapEx." SpaceX and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) sit at about 275 basis points, "with buildouts increasingly reliant on outside funding."

That means insuring SpaceX's debt costs about 3.4x as much as insuring Microsoft's.

This week's bond sale backs that up. SpaceX sold $32 billion of debt backed by Nvidia chips, and people familiar with the sale say the biggest piece, about $25.2 billion, priced at 8.259%. The average US high-grade bond yielded 5.95% that day, according to Bloomberg's index data.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on SpaceX, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See SpaceX's Analyst Ratings

Analysts don't see the cash flow yet

CFO Bret Johnsen said this week that much of the 10 gigawatts SpaceX plans to build next year will be funded from internal cash flows, as another investor relayed it on X. Analysts' estimates show far more cash going out than coming in:

SpaceX (SPCX): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2026-2028 (TIKR)

That adds up to nearly $270 billion of negative free cash flow from 2026 through 2028, with $146 billion of it in 2027, the year of the 10-gigawatt build. SpaceX held $89.9 billion of cash and marketable securities at Sept. 30, and it has guided to $35 billion to $40 billion of capex in the fourth quarter alone.
